newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia contests US criticism on treatment of Serbs.
newsitem.headline: Croatia contests US criticism on treatment of Serbs.

text.p: Croatia on Friday appeared to challenge U.S. criticism over its treatment of minority Serbs displaced by war, saying it needed economic aid to enable them to return to their homes.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday met a visiting Croatian delegation and brought up several contentious issues, including Croatia's failure to allow Serbs to return to their homes in the former rebel Krajina region of the country.
Her criticism coincided with reports of harassment and expulsions of elderly Serbs by Bosnian Croat refugees now being resettled in former Serb homes by the Zagreb government.

Albright reiterated warnings that Croatia's keen desire to become fully integrated into the West -- including membership in key institutions and access to international financing -- could be jeopardised if Zagreb failed to meet its commitments under the 1995 Dayton Accords, which ended wars in former Yugoslavia.
Foreign Minister Mate Granic told Croatian state television on Friday that "Croatia will give full protection to the Serb minority" and would look into every incident.
But Jure Radic, Minister for Reconstruction and Development, hinted that Zagreb could not readily comply with all U.S. demands.

"We don't want to single out the problems pertaining only to the return of the Serbs. We are talking about the return of all the displaced," Radic told state radio reporters in Washington, referring to Croatian war refugees as well.
"Our list of priorities doesn't put a Serb or a Croat on top of the list but those who have suffered in the war -- orphans, invalids and so on," he said.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Thursday that Albright "did not refer specifically to any kind of financial penalties".

But Burns noted that Washington recently abstained on Croatia's bid for an International Monetary Fund loan to nudge Zagreb into extraditing an indicted Croat war criminal to the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
The indictee was extradited two weeks ago.
Radic said that Zagreb "respects America's concern for democratic principles in Croatia" but "there must be economic aid behind that concern.
"We can't implement the entire programme without additional financial aid from the world, to help us reconstruct at least another 50,000 houses," Radic said.
U.S. officials said Granic and other Croatian officials were extremely defensive during the Washington meeting and Albright did not receive a satisfactory response to her complaints.

There are up to 180,000 refugees in Croatia now, about 60,000 of them Serbs who fled their rebel Krajina region in 1995 and settled in the last Serb enclave, Eastern Slavonia, and some 80,000 Croats driven out by fighting there in 1991.
Eastern Slavonia, a once affluent region dominated by Serbs and bordering the Yugoslav republic of Serbia, is administered by the United Nations, whose mandate expires on July 15.

It will then revert to Croatian central government control. Croatia is keen to move its Croatian refugees back to Eastern Slavonia but Western officials say this means Serb refugees must be allowed to return home in the old Krajina region.
